items.title: AI Chip Stocks Bounce After Steep Selloff; AMD Soars Over 11% in a Day, Philadelphia Semiconductor Index Rebounds 4.21% but Still Plunges 15% for the Week - BigGo Finance
items.summary: AI Chip Stocks Bounce After Steep Selloff; AMD Soars Over 11% in a Day, Philadelphia Semiconductor Index Rebounds 4.21% but Still Plunges 15% for the Week  BigGo Finance
items.content:
AI Chip Stocks Bounce After Steep Selloff; AMD Soars Over 11% in a Day, Philadelphia Semiconductor Index Rebounds 4.21% but Still Plunges 15% for the Week
After an epic selloff, U.S. AI and chip stocks staged a rebound from steep losses last Friday, with AMD surging 11.04% in a single day and Intel climbing 7.71%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 4.21%, but the Nasdaq and S&P 500 still ended the week lower, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 15.36% for the week. Strong October nonfarm payrolls data pushed the probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December to about 78%, capping the rebound. The market largely attributes the selling wave to hedge fund deleveraging and mechanical selling rather than deteriorating AI fundamentals, but data center regulatory concerns and downward revisions to Anthropic and OpenAI valuation expectations are keeping investors cautious about the AI trade.
AMD Nvidia Intel Micron Technology Philadelphia Semiconductor Index TSMC ADR Anthropic OpenAI Federal Reserve (Fed) CoreWeave
After five days of heavy selling, U.S. technology stocks rebounded last Friday (the 6th), led by chip and artificial intelligence (AI) stocks. AMD soared 11.04% in a single day and Intel climbed 7.71%, lifting the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index 4.21%. However, the rebound was not enough to recover the previous day's losses, and all four major indexes ended the week lower, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunging 15.36%, indicating that correction pressure on the AI complex has not truly eased.
At the close of New York trading on the 6th, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 237.33 points, or 0.46%, to 51,285.73, its lowest since October 15. The S&P 500 rose 23.13 points, or 0.31%, to 7,376.86. The Nasdaq gained 264.43 points, or 1.09%, to 24,579.42. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which had plunged 12.25% just the previous trading day, rebounded 379.11 points, or 4.21%, to 9,390.25.
Semiconductor stocks led the rebound. AMD closed at $449.04, up more than 11%; Intel closed at $56.28, up more than 7%; Micron Technology rose 5.1%, Qualcomm gained more than 5%, Arm rose 4.74%, and Broadcom edged up 0.74%. Nvidia surged as much as 7.3% intraday before paring gains to close up 2.78% at $186.64, still the best performer among Dow components. TSMC's ADR rebounded 6.33% to $375.44 (about NT$12,000), and United Microelectronics' ADR rose 3.51% to $13.85 (about NT$450), but neither recovered the losses from the previous trading day, when they plunged 10.78% and 16.69%, respectively.
Large technology stocks diverged. Microsoft fell about 1%. Oracle, after reports that Microsoft would not renew leases for some AI computing resources, fell as much as 5.2% intraday before closing up about 0.8%.
The U.S. Labor Department reported Friday that October nonfarm payrolls increased by 165,000, far above the market expectation of 70,000, while the September increase was revised up to 60,000. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2%, and average hourly earnings rose 3.1% year over year, also above the estimated 2.9%. The labor market's resilience eased concerns about an economic slowdown but deepened investors' worries about inflation and the interest rate outlook.
After the data were released, traders' bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike in December increased markedly. According to LSEG data, the market-implied probability of a rate hike next month rose to 78% from 70% previously, and U.S. Treasury yields rose in tandem. New York Fed President John Williams said inflation remains too high, but other economic indicators have not yet sent worrying signals, and the central bank still needs to assess price risks based on subsequent data.
Selloff Stemmed From Leverage Adjustment, Not Deteriorating Fundamentals
Market participants generally view the rebound on the 6th as closer to short covering and dip buying, not yet enough to confirm that a bottom has formed. According to a MarketWatch report, StoneX analyst Yi Fu Lee noted that Thursday's sharp selloff in chip stocks actually created an obvious short-term rebound opportunity for positioning in AI-related chip stocks on Friday. He compared the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX), which plunged 12% on Thursday, with the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV), which tracks technology software stocks and fell only about 4%.
Stifel analyst Brian Chin described Friday's move as a "sharp volatility reversal," saying that while chip stocks rebounded, uncertainty over future data center spending will not fade quickly and could continue to drive share price volatility in the near term. He also noted, however, that the U.S. midterm elections did not change the market's fundamental demand for AI; what has become more complicated is the regulatory environment for related industries.
Some institutions characterize the correction as position adjustment rather than an industry turning point. Goldman Sachs data showed that the net leverage ratio measuring hedge funds' long and short positions fell to 73.4% in October, down 4.2 percentage points from the previous month, the largest monthly decline since March, with technology stocks seeing about $20 billion (about NT$660 billion) in net selling over the past two weeks. Morgan Stanley also noted that October's reduction in equity hedge fund positions was the largest in more than a decade. JPMorgan analysis found that as major indexes weakened on the 5th, selling by trend-following funds (CTAs) intensified in tandem, with leveraged ETFs estimated to have sold more than $60 billion (about NT$2 trillion) of stocks before the close, about 90% of it concentrated in technology-related products such as semiconductors and the Nasdaq 100.
Deutsche Bank believes the decline in large technology stocks was excessive and has upgraded its investment rating, while Wells Fargo said investors are beginning to scrutinize companies' returns on AI investment and their ability to monetize it.
Data Center Regulatory Concerns and Cooling AI Valuations
After Democrats won a landslide in the midterm elections, concerns about tighter data center regulation intensified. Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of Texas, had promised stricter regulation during her campaign, but in a CNN interview last Thursday her tone softened, saying she is not opposed to data centers but wants to pause current construction until supporting measures to protect Texas residents are in place.
J. Gold Associates analyst Jack Gold believes the market overreacted to the Democratic victory, with some investors even interpreting the election results as the imminent end of data center construction. He said the selloff was too large and some investors are now buying at low prices. Lior Prosor, managing partner at venture capital firm Deep33, noted that even if U.S. data center construction slows temporarily, it does not mean AI companies' revenue will necessarily decline in coming quarters; computing capacity originally available could instead meet demand in other regions, because demand for computing power is global.
Valuation expectations in the primary market have also loosened. It is understood that Anthropic plans to launch its IPO roadshow next week, and some potential investors have cut their expectations for its listing valuation to $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion, down 35% to 40% from the previous expectation of up to $2 trillion. OpenAI has similarly lowered its valuation expectation in a new funding round, from a previously planned maximum of $1.5 trillion to $1.25 trillion, and has cut the size of the raise by at least one-third from the initially planned maximum of $30 billion (about NT$980 billion). People familiar with the matter said OpenAI still expects to complete this round within the coming weeks, planning to raise up to $20 billion (about NT$660 billion) in two tranches.
Still, there are positive signals on the AI demand side. The Wall Street Journal reported that Anthropic's annualized recurring revenue (ARR) had exceeded $80 billion (about NT$2.6 trillion) as of the end of October, higher than at the end of September.
LPL Financial chief strategist Adam Turnquist said AI has been put to the test many times during this rally but has always overcome doubts and passed, and this week's market reaction seems overly sensitive. Mark Spindel, a partner at Pilot Wave Holdings, believes the market on Thursday concentrated various concerns—AI capital spending, data center policy risk, inflation and rising rates—into a single wave of trading, and Friday's rebound shows investors are beginning to distinguish among these risks rather than treating them as a single problem. He stressed that chip demand has not disappeared, but short-term volatility is inevitable as investors reassess the timetable for AI infrastructure buildout.
JPMorgan believes large-scale deleveraging may have peaked and funding conditions will gradually improve. The market will next focus closely on the earnings report of AI infrastructure company CoreWeave on the 10th; only if AI infrastructure investment demand and memory price outlook remain solid will the semiconductor rally have a chance to continue. Until then, data center construction policy, AI companies' investment returns and the Federal Reserve's rate path will remain the three major variables driving technology stocks.

Lisa Nandy wary of ‘circular arguments’ about rejoining EU
Culture secretary pushes back against talk of revisiting Brexit but says closer ties would fulfil referendum promises
One of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said she wants to avoid “circular arguments” about whether the UK should rejoin the EU, underlining divisions at the top of government over revisiting Brexit .
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, appeared to suggest she was not in favour of rejoining the trade bloc, but she said the prime minister should still pursue closer ties to fulfil the promises made at the time of the referendum.
She is one of a handful of cabinet ministers who are concerned about Burnham’s plan for an “honest conversation” with the public about Brexit and who are privately warning it could reopen a row that would only benefit Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.
“I do not believe that anybody wants to repeat circular arguments about in or out, leave or remain. I do think, though, that over the last decade we have let the British people down very badly,” she told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.
Five European leaders call for closer EU-UK ties ahead of Brussels summit
Nandy, whose Wigan seat voted overwhelmingly for leave in 2016, and who is one of the most cautious in the cabinet about reversing Brexit, was asked if she wanted to go back in. “I don’t know if that’s a choice we have,” she said.
However, she did concede that Burnham was trying to address the failings of the Brexit deal, telling Sky News it was important to “be honest” and highlight that “the deal that we got is not what we were promised”.
The culture secretary stressed there were “trade-offs and choices” to be made which involved a conversation with people across the country, indicating that Brexit would be a key theme of the next election campaign.
Burnham will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday. Downing Street sources said he would use it to get Labour’s reset deal over the line and to meet many European leaders for the first time.
In private, EU counterparts will be expecting Burnham to set out his ambitions for further integration after he announced his intention to move beyond Labour’s “red lines” on the bloc after the next election.
At a Brexit reset meeting on 20 November in Brussels, agreements on agriculture and food, emissions trading and youth experience visas are expected to be confirmed.
Burnham said at the weekend there was more to come. “This summit will show what we can achieve when we work together, but it doesn’t need to be the end of our ambition,” he told the Sunday Mirror.
Officials will also discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, which could include another attempt for the UK to join the EU’s €150bn (£125bn) Safe defence fund , collaboration on law enforcement and borders, and visas for touring artists.
Soon after the Brussels summit, Burnham is expected to give a speech setting out options for a closer relationship with the EU, arguing it would be in the UK’s long-term interest. No 10 sources said he wanted to “frame the conversation, not go straight to the endgame” before testing public opinion.
Senior government figures say Burnham wants a mandate to start negotiations with the EU in Labour’s next election manifesto, but that any subsequent referendum would be solely confirmatory.
“You can’t ask people to vote on an undefined plan like in 2016. That was David Cameron’s mistake,” one said.
However, Burnham has faced reservations from others within his cabinet. The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, are cautious about pushing to fully rejoin.
The EU’s former chief Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier said London could not have the “single market à la carte” by cherrypicking which of the four freedoms – including freedom of movement – it would like in future negotiations.
“There is no cherrypicking. There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other,” he told the BBC.
Nandy was forced to reject allegations that celebrating the UK rejoining the Erasmus plus scheme by linking it to Remembrance Sunday was inappropriate, after suggesting it would help to honour “the immense courage of those who served our country” before Remembrance Sunday.
Kevin Hollinrake, the Tory chair, suggested she was using the national civic occasion to “try to make an EU membership pitch”. He said: “Our veterans did not fight for a student exchange scheme.”
Speaking on Sky News, Nandy responded: “They are the only party that is talking about Brexit and the EU. What we are announcing this weekend is that we’re going to widen the Erasmus scheme.
“I cannot see what is political about saying that we want young people from every part of this country to understand the contribution that their grandparents and great-grandparents made, not just to us but to many, many lives of people that they had never met,” she added.

Here are the 2 big things we're watching in the stock market in the week ahead
There's one question on everybody's mind entering the new trading week: Where are artificial intelligence stocks going next? The engine of the four-year-old bull market is coming off a bruising week , sparked by the midterm elections, when gubernatorial candidates who support restrictions on data center development won big in states like Texas and Ohio. Voters across the country also approved local ballot measures that could slow the pace of AI investment and construction. As Jim Cramer made clear at Friday's Annual Meeting , this is a real risk to the future earnings of chipmakers, electrical equipment suppliers and other companies with brimming order books to support the AI buildout. We take it seriously and may need to make further adjustments to our stock portfolio to reduce AI exposure. This headwind didn't blow in from nowhere. It's why we exited Corning in early September and Broadcom in late October , and two months ago initiated positions in the non-tech stocks of Kimberly-Clark and Bank of New York . The upshot after such a whirlwind week for the market? No Club holdings are reporting in the coming days and the economic calendar is also fairly light. Here's a closer look at what to expect: 1. AI earnings: Neocloud CoreWeave's earnings report on Tuesday night will help determine whether the AI trade can regain momentum. Even before the election, we've been paying close attention to CoreWeave's bonds and stock as a barometer for souring investor appetite for AI names. How the market responds to CoreWeave's results and commentary on the conference call could have far-reaching implications. "That's going to be the one," Jim said at the Annual Meeting. "You either believe [CEO Michael Intrator] and you see the stock go up and you realize that the AI trade is on. Or you don't believe Michael and the stock plummets, and it'll be a really bad day. ... CoreWeave is so important. It's insanely important." On Thursday morning, CoreWeave's peer in the neocloud game, Nebius , delivers earnings of its own. And that evening, networking giant Cisco Systems and chipmaking equipment supplier Applied Materials will release quarterly results. How Big Oil Became the AI Industry's Favorite Customer
OpenAI, ADNOC and G42 signed a multi-year deal on Nov. 2 to put AI across the Abu Dhabi oil company's operations, the highest-profile example of tech firms pitching bespoke tools to oil clients at ADIPEC, Semafor reports.
The traffic runs both ways: Microsoft has a 20-year gas power deal with Chevron for a planned 2.67-gigawatt West Texas plant, and Amazon's planned Texas plant could become the country's biggest single emitter if built to its permit limits.
A peer-reviewed modeling study estimates that AI gains in fossil fuels would add 0.47 billion to 1.8 billion metric tons of CO2 a year even if renewables gain equally, with the low end comparable to Mexico's annual emissions, co-author Holly Alpine says.
Artificial intelligence companies are deepening their ties with the fossil fuel industries as some of the biggest names in the tech world make massive deals with energy companies, both to power their energy-hungry data centers and to embed machine learning into the energy sector itself. Already, the artificial intelligence boom is causing a natural gas surge in the United States, and experts expect that data center hyperscalers will greatly extend the life of fossil fuels in the global energy mix, even as the world continues to shatter clean energy growth records.
This Monday, OpenAI – the firm behind ChatGPT – made a deal with Abu Dhabi's ADNOC “to deploy advanced AI capabilities across the state energy firm's operations,” according to reporting from Reuters. The report noted that the agreement “mark[s] the latest step in the ChatGPT maker's deepening ties with the United Arab Emirates.”
But the trend extends far beyond just one firm and one country. Globally, AI firms are racing to make products designed for some of the richest pockets in the world – oil and gas companies. A recent report from nonpartisan global news outlet Semafor notes that the OpenAI-ADNOC deal “was the highest-profile example in a broader push at ADIPEC by tech companies to pitch bespoke, AI-driven tools to help operate drilling rigs, refineries, and other oil assets.”
What is more, the deepening ties between AI and fossil fuels goes both ways. Big Tech is planning data centers faster than global power grids can keep up. Plus, legislation under the Trump administration has pushed tech companies to provide their own energy sources to power new planned data centers, leaving Silicon Valley scrambling to add energy production capacity by any means necessary. While this includes funding research and development of next-gen clean energy technologies like nuclear fusion and space-based solar power, in practice it has translated to massive natural gas contracts.
At present, Amazon is constructing a gas-fired power plant in Texas that, if completed according to the current plan involving the development of seven natural gas plants, will be the single-biggest source of power-related emissions in the entire United States . In August, AI giant Nvidia announced that it would partner with Japan’s SoftBank and the United States federal government to build the largest fossil-fuel plant in the country in order to power an Ohio project by OpenAI. Microsoft, too, just signed a 20-year deal with Chevron to provide 2.67 gigawatts of natural-gas-fired power for a proposed West Texas data center.
AI advocates argue that in the long run, AI will save more energy than it consumes thanks to efficiency gains across all of the sectors that use it. However, those gains are a double-edged sword. A recent paper published by NPJ Climate Action found that, if fossil fuels make economic gains anywhere above zero thanks to AI integration, enabled emissions will exceed avoided emissions. In a scenario where both the fossil fuel and the renewables sector benefit equally from AI gains, global CO2 emissions will still increase by between 0.47 billion tons and 1.8 billion tons a year. “On the smaller side it's about the emissions of Mexico annually,” Holly Alpine, one of the co-authors of the research, was recently quoted by the Wall Street Journal.
Despite NPJ Climate Action’s sobering warning, AI firms are tripping over themselves to court fossil fuel companies and secure long-term contracts with economic heavyweights in Big Oil. The OpenAI-ADNOC deal is not the first of its kind, but the high-profile nature of the agreement is indicative of the direction that the sectors as a whole are heading – and it’s not good for anyone’s bottom line but their own.

If the Fed Raises Interest Rates in December, I'm Making This 1 Investing Move
The Federal Open Market Committee decided not to raise interest rates when it last met on Oct. 28, but a rate hike in December is expected.
In the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC) last summary of projections, members targeted a year-end median federal funds rate of 4.1%. The rate is currently in the 3.75% to 4% range, so their median projections would suggest one more rate hike this year.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Does that mean the Federal Reserve will raise rates when it meets next on Dec. 8-9? No, but based on the fact that inflation keeps rising and the FOMC itself said it was likely, it is widely anticipated.
At the time of this writing, the CME FedWatch survey says that 68% of interest rate traders expect a rate hike in December, while 32% say that rates will hold. No one sees rates declining in December.
As for the longer-term projections, the dotplot indicates that rates will be at 4.1% in 2027, which means they see no movement next year, assuming a rate hike in December. The CME FedWatch poll says 34% expect rates at 4.25% to 4.50% a year from now, in December 2027. That would indicate two rate hikes from the current range.
Some 33% say rates will be at 4% to 4.25% next year, while 11% say they will be where they are now, 3.75% to 4%. Only 1% anticipate rates declining in 2027 to the 3.50% to 3.75% range.
While these projections are subject to change, investors should anticipate that rates will rise in December and stay high at least through 2027 -- and likely beyond. Should that alter your investment strategy?
As a long-term investor, the fluctuating interest rate should not, in itself, signal that any major portfolio moves need to be made.
That seems particularly true in this case. This does not appear to be the beginning of a Fed tightening regime like we saw in 2022. In 2022, inflation was rising rapidly and rates had been at 0%, so it was clear that rates would be moving steadily higher for quite a while to cool down inflation.
This is a very different environment. Rates had already started to come down as inflation had been under control, but tariffs followed by the war in Iran and its impact on energy prices has begun to move inflation higher.
But the Fed has given no indication in its dotplot or statements that this is the start of an aggressive plan to hike rates. It is more likely that rates will hover around where they are now, maybe moving slightly higher, but staying roughly where they are, at least in 2027. It's what many call a higher-for-longer scenario.
Of course, things can change ... just like they did last year. In December 2025, rates were lowered to 3.50% to 3.75% and the expectation was for one rate cut in 2026 to 3.25% to 3.50%, and one more rate cut in 2027 to 3% to 3.25%. But, the war in Iran happened and instead of a rate cut, we got a rate hike.
With the Democrats winning the House and Senate on Nov. 3, there is strong sentiment to end the war, eliminate the Trump tariff increases, and rebuild trade relationships. This could potentially bring down prices and lead to rate cuts instead of rate hikes. And it may not -- but the point is, these projections are not set in stone and could certainly change.
That's why, as an investor, the first thing I would do if the FOMC raises rates in December is to sit tight and do nothing.
This doesn't appear to be the start of aggressive rate tightening, and it is likely that rates will hold steady for a while. There is even a chance that they start to move back down next year.
Even before the election, the FOMC, in its September dotplot, expected inflation to be down to 2.3% at the end of 2027, so there is an expectation for declining inflation -- and that would be a good thing for rates.
But in the broader view, even if rates dipped in 2027, it will probably not be a major shift. You should be prepared for a stable, but higher-for-longer rate environment.
At the end of 2027, after the FOMC acts, investors should review their portfolios as a matter of course. This is especially true with a new Congress coming in and new policies. There could certainly be some changes afoot that impact your portfolio at the margins, but right now it's too early to tell.
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.
But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.
While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

International gold prices extended their decline as a strong U.S. labor market reinforced expectations for further Fed rate hikes .
Stronger October U.S. job growth and a rise in the consumer sentiment index increased the odds of further monetary tightening , which could reduce the appeal of non-yielding gold during a period of rising interest rates .
The direction of gold prices will hinge on the U.S. consumer price index (CPI) due on Nov. 10, which will test whether safe-haven demand can overcome the drag from dollar strength on gold.
Gold extended its decline as strength in the U.S. labor market bolstered expectations for further Federal Reserve interest-rate increases.
Bloomberg reported on Nov. 8 that spot gold traded at around $4,070 an ounce. Bullion fell 0.4% on Nov. 6, then slipped another 0.1% to $4,065.58 an ounce as of 7:35 a.m. Singapore time on Nov. 9.
The move followed stronger-than-expected U.S. employment data for October, which increased the likelihood of further monetary tightening. Nonfarm payrolls rose by 165,000, beating market forecasts, while the unemployment rate edged lower. Consumer sentiment in early November also climbed to its highest level in three months.
Markets are focused on whether the Fed will raise its benchmark rate at the December Federal Open Market Committee meeting. Persistent inflation pressure tied to high energy prices, along with solid employment data, is supporting the case for tighter policy. Because gold does not pay interest, it tends to become less attractive when rates rise.
Gold had earlier recovered the $4,000-an-ounce level after the U.S. midterm elections. Safe-haven demand increased as U.S. Treasury yields and crude prices fell on expectations that Democratic control of Congress would raise hopes for an end to the Iran war and limit additional fiscal spending. Even so, gold remains down about 20% since clashes between the U.S. and Iran began in late February.
Hebe Chen, a market analyst at Vantage Global Prime, said safe-haven demand and dollar strength are pulling the gold market in opposite directions. Gold has kept its safe-haven status, but the stronger dollar is limiting further gains.
The next key variable for gold is the U.S. consumer price index due on Nov. 10. Chen said the inflation data will test whether safe-haven demand can overcome the restraint that dollar strength has placed on gold prices.
At the same time, spot silver fell 0.2% to $51.81 an ounce. Platinum and palladium edged higher. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, which tracks the U.S. currency against major peers, rose 0.4% in the previous session.
